title: The Three-Point Revolution: How One Shot Changed Basketball Forever
summary: The three-point line has existed in the NBA since 1979. For decades it was a novelty. Then Stephen Curry happened — and basketball was never the same again. We trace the revolution that transformed how the game is played and valued.
content:
In the 1979-80 NBA season, the first year the three-point line was used, the entire league averaged 2.8 three-point attempts per game. In the 2022-23 season, teams averaged 34.2 attempts per game. That shift — from novelty to cornerstone of offensive strategy — is one of the most dramatic tactical evolutions in the history of any major sport.

The three-point revolution did not happen overnight. It was a gradual realisation, accelerated by one player above all others, that shooting from beyond the arc was not just a desperation option but potentially the most efficient shot in basketball.

The Mathematics

The logic is simple once you see it. A team that shoots 35% from three-point range scores 1.05 points per attempt. A team that shoots 50% from two-point range — a good but not exceptional rate — scores 1.0 points per attempt. The three-point shot, even at a significantly lower percentage than a two, produces more points per possession.

This mathematical reality was understood by analysts long before it reshaped the game. What changed was the willingness of coaches and players to act on it — and the emergence of players skilled enough to make three-pointers at the rates needed to validate the strategy.

Stephen Curry: The Catalyst

Stephen Curry did not invent the three-point shot. But he transformed it. His range — shooting accurately from distances that other elite shooters would not attempt — forced defences to guard him at points on the court where no previous player had needed to be guarded. This created space for his teammates and options for Golden State's offence that defences had no precedent for handling.

Curry's back-to-back MVP seasons in 2015 and 2016, the second of which was unanimous — the first unanimous MVP in NBA history — validated a style of play that had previously been dismissed as gimmicky. Teams watched Golden State win championships and began rebuilding their rosters around shooting.

Curry didn't just change how teams used the three-point shot. He changed what defences had to do to guard it — and that changed everything about how space was created on a basketball court.

The Ripple Effects

The three-point revolution changed not just shooting but every other aspect of basketball strategy. The midrange jumper — the pull-up two-pointer from 15-18 feet — became widely considered the least efficient shot in basketball and largely disappeared from elite offences. Big men who couldn't shoot from outside became less valuable; versatile forwards who could shoot threes became premium assets.

Defensive schemes had to adapt — dropping back in pick-and-roll coverage (which conceded open threes) became untenable, forcing switches that created mismatches. The game became faster, more spread out, and more reliant on shooting skill than at any previous point in its history.

Has It Gone Too Far?

Some basketball purists argue that the three-point revolution has simplified the game — that the emphasis on shooting has come at the cost of the post play, the midrange artistry, and the interior physical battles that made basketball great. Players like Nikola Jokic and Joel Embiid, who have demonstrated that elite post play is still viable, have offered an alternative vision of basketball excellence.

The reality is probably that the game has found a new equilibrium — one in which three-point shooting is central but not exclusive, and in which the most effective offences combine spacing, shooting, and interior threat in ways that defences cannot solve with any single approach.
